Segment Selection With Evidence

The Commercial SystemPart 3

By lowob · 10 July 2026 · 9-minute read · Strategy

Segment selection is the decision about which groups of buyers the firm pursues first, which it serves when they arrive, and which it declines. Most firms make it on market size and logo appeal. The better evidence is usually in the CRM already: win rate, deal size, cycle length and retention by segment, combined into a value per opportunity. Gartner's research on key accounts found that customers elevated mainly for their large spend were 51% less likely to increase it over time, a reminder that size is not the same as potential. Choose on evidence, check the chosen segment is large enough from the bottom up, and record the choice with its disqualifiers and a review date.

Part 2 of this series argued that a position starts with a named buyer. This piece is about choosing that buyer from evidence. It is the most consequential decision in the Strategy part of the commercial system, because every later part inherits it: Growth targets the segment, Distribution chooses partners who reach it and Revenue qualifies against it.

A segment, here, is a group of potential buyers who share the characteristics that change how they buy: sector, size, situation, the problem they have and the route by which they purchase. A segment is narrower than a market and broader than an ideal customer profile. The profile describes the best accounts inside the chosen segment (How to write an ICP).

Why most segment choices are made on size

The usual process starts with a market report, a total addressable market figure and a slide showing the firm's share of it. That process answers a real question, whether the segment is big enough to matter, but it is the second question, not the first.

Wing VC's guide to market sizing describes top-down sizing as starting from public industry data and narrowing with filters, and notes that industry sources are not always available or current in fast-moving markets. For emerging technology firms that caveat is often decisive. The category may not exist in any report yet.

The bias toward size also distorts account choice. Gartner research reported in 2021 found that customers elevated to key-account status mainly because of their large spend were 51% less likely to increase that spend over time, and that 58% of B2B sales organisations missed key-account quota. Large is attractive. It is not evidence of fit.

QuestionTop-down sizing answers itWin-loss and CRM evidence answers it
Does the segment exist and is it large?YesPartly
Can we win there?NoYes
How fast do deals close?NoYes
Do customers stay and expand?NoYes
Can we reach buyers through channels we have?NoPartly

The evidence the firm already holds

Most firms with 20 or more customers can rank segments from their own records. Four numbers do most of the work.

Win rate by segment. Closed-won divided by closed-won plus closed-lost, including no-decision losses, over the last four to eight quarters.

Deal size. First-year contract value, using realised price after discounts.

Cycle length. Days from qualified opportunity to close. Ebsta's 2024 benchmarks, drawn from 4.2 million opportunities at 530 companies, found that win rates fell 67% when deals slipped, especially beyond eight weeks. Long cycles carry a hidden cost beyond time.

Retention. Gross and net revenue retention for the segment's customers. SaaS Capital's 2025 benchmarks found net retention rises with contract value, with a median of 102% for contracts of $25,000 to $50,000. Growth Unhinged's 2025 survey of more than 800 software firms found companies with high net retention and short CAC payback grew at 71% on average, against 10% for those weak on both.

Ebsta's analysis adds one behavioural finding: top performers prioritise the accounts and personas they have closed before. The best sellers already select segments from evidence. The firm's job is to make that selection explicit.

Scoring segments: a worked method

Combine the four numbers into a single figure: expected value per opportunity-month. It rewards segments that win often, pay well, close quickly and stay.

Expected value per opportunity-month = win rate × first-year value × gross retention ÷ cycle length in months.

Segment (illustrative)Win rateFirst-year valueGross retentionCycle (months)Value per opportunity-month
A: mid-size operators with a regulatory trigger30%$40,00090%4$2,700
B: large enterprises, central IT buyer18%$90,00085%9$1,530
C: small firms, founder buyer40%$15,00070%2$2,100

Segment B has the largest deals and would lead most board slides. On evidence, A is the better first choice: each month a seller spends on an A opportunity is worth almost twice a month on a B opportunity. Segment C wins most often but churns.

Two adjustments keep the score honest. First, add cost to serve where it differs materially: onboarding effort, support load or required customisation. Second, add a reach factor. A segment the firm cannot reach through channels it already has will need investment in Distribution before the score is realised. Ebsta found partnership channels returned 3.8 times the velocity, yet only 8% of businesses had one.

The largest deals are rarely the best segment. The best segment is where a seller's month is worth most.

Sizing what you chose, from the bottom up

Once a segment ranks well, check it is large enough. Bottom-up sizing starts from the firm's own numbers rather than an industry total. Wing VC's guide describes it as average price multiplied by the number of buyers, and notes it needs some sales history to work.

A worked check for segment A:

StepFigure (illustrative)Source
Accounts meeting the segment filters1,200Company registry or data provider, filtered
Share showing the trigger in a year25%, or 300 accountsTrigger tracking, past deal history
Accounts the team can engage in a year100Seller capacity and channel reach
Win rate30%CRM
New customers per year30100 × 30%
New first-year value$1.2m30 × $40,000

If $1.2m of new business a year meets the plan, the segment is sufficient. If not, the constraint is visible: more capacity, a channel that widens reach, or a second segment. The calculation also names the assumption most worth testing, here the 25% trigger rate.

When there is not enough data

Firms with fewer than ten customers cannot rank segments statistically. That is normal for early emerging technology firms, and the answer is not to choose on size by default. It is to treat the choice as a hypothesis with a test that could disprove it (First customers in a market that doesn't exist yet).

A useful test has a fixed budget, a fixed period and a pre-agreed result that would change the decision. Our piece on testing sets out how to design one (Tests that close questions).

Evidence availableWhat to do
Fewer than 10 customersChoose one segment as a hypothesis; run 20 to 30 qualified conversations; record why each did or did not progress
10 to 30 customersRank segments on win rate and cycle length; treat retention as provisional
More than 30 customers with a year of historyUse the full score, with cost to serve and reach
Any size, entering a new segmentScore it on comparable segments and set an earlier review date

Forrester's 2023 analysis found that clients who brought three or more buying-group members into the sales process saw a 50% increase in meeting-to-close conversion. For a segment test, that suggests a practical rule: count a conversation as evidence only if it reached more than one role.

Record the choice and the disqualifiers

A segment choice is a strategic decision and belongs in the decision record: the segments chosen, the segments declined, the score and the assumptions behind it, the owner, the expected win rate and cycle length, and a review date (The ten commercial decisions worth recording).

The declined segments matter as much as the chosen one. Disqualifiers stop sellers spending months on deals that will not close or will churn. When a declined-segment deal does arrive, the record makes the exception visible: someone can still take it, but on the record, with a reason. Over a year, those exceptions become evidence for the next review.

This is where segment selection meets The Build Order. Agents that score inbound leads, draft outreach or prepare account briefs need the segment definition and disqualifiers as rules they can read. A brain that has them qualifies consistently. One that does not reproduces each seller's private judgment.

Illustrative example: choosing the smaller deals
Decision
Make mid-size operators with a regulatory trigger the primary segment for the next two quarters, and stop outbound to large enterprises with a central IT buyer.
Reason and owner
Segment scoring on six quarters of CRM data showed almost twice the value per opportunity-month, driven by a shorter cycle and higher win rate. Owned by the commercial lead; agreed by the founders.
What changed
Outbound lists, partner briefs and qualification criteria were rewritten; enterprise deals that arrive inbound are taken as recorded exceptions; the review is set for two quarters out.

Illustrative: a composite of an 80-person emerging technology firm, built from patterns across engagements.

lowob takeaways

  • Size tells you a segment exists, not that you can win it. Rank on win rate, deal size, cycle length and retention.
  • Score value per seller-month. It exposes segments with large deals that consume the team.
  • Size from the bottom up. Accounts, triggers, capacity and win rate show whether the segment is big enough and which assumption to test.
  • Record what you decline. Disqualifiers and recorded exceptions are the evidence for the next review.
Gateway card

Before you commit to a segment

  • Win rate, deal size, cycle length and retention calculated per segment
  • Cost to serve and reach noted where they differ materially
  • A bottom-up check showing the segment meets the plan
  • The weakest assumption named, with a way to test it
  • Declined segments and disqualifiers written down
  • The choice recorded with an owner and a review date

Common questions

How do you choose a target market segment in B2B?

Rank candidate segments on win rate, deal size, cycle length and retention from your own CRM, then check the best-ranked segment is large enough using bottom-up sizing.

What is the difference between a segment and an ideal customer profile?

A segment is a group of buyers who share characteristics that change how they buy. An ideal customer profile describes the best accounts within the chosen segment, including disqualifiers.

Is top-down or bottom-up market sizing better?

They answer different questions. Top-down shows whether a market is large; bottom-up, built from your own prices and win rates, shows what you can realistically capture.

How do you choose a segment with very few customers?

Treat it as a hypothesis. Pick one segment, run a fixed number of qualified conversations within a set period, and agree in advance what result would change the decision.

Next move

Export the last six quarters of closed deals, tag each with a segment, and calculate win rate and cycle length for each. If the ranking surprises the team, that is the conversation to have before the next planning cycle.
